name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q01 - Chronological order of cell theory milestones

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following historical milestones in cell biology in the correct chronological order from earliest to latest:

A. Theodore Schwann proposed that the bodies of animals and plants are composed of cells and products of cells.
B. Anton Von Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell.
C. Rudolf Virchow explained that new cells are formed from pre-existing cells.
D. Matthias Schleiden observed that all plants are composed of different kinds of cells.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The understanding of cellular organisation and the formulation of cell theory developed sequentially through microscopic observations and comparative studies of plant and animal tissues.

Step 2: Chronological Evaluation of Events
First, Anton Von Leeuwenhoek saw and described a live cell. Later, in 1838, Matthias Schleiden examined a large number of plants and observed that all plants are composed of different kinds of cells forming plant tissues. At about the same time, in 1839, Theodore Schwann studied animal cells and plant tissues, proposing that the bodies of animals and plants are composed of cells and products of cells. Finally, in 1855, Rudolf Virchow modified the hypothesis of Schleiden and Schwann by explaining that cells divide and new cells are formed from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence from earliest to latest is: Anton Von Leeuwenhoek describing a live cell, followed by Matthias Schleiden (1838), then Theodore Schwann (1839), and finally Rudolf Virchow (1855), which corresponds to B, D, A, C.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q02 - Sequence of protein processing in Golgi

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following events of protein synthesis, packaging, and modification in the endomembrane system in the correct logical sequence:

A. Modification of proteins within the cisternae of the Golgi apparatus.
B. Release of modified materials from the trans face of the Golgi apparatus.
C. Synthesis of proteins by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
D. Fusion of vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum with the cis face of the Golgi apparatus.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Within the endomembrane system, the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) and the Golgi apparatus work in close coordination to synthesise, modify, and package proteins for intracellular targets or secretion.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Pathway Analysis
The process begins with the synthesis of proteins by ribosomes attached to the surface of the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Materials to be packaged are then transported in the form of vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum and fuse with the convex cis (forming) face of the Golgi apparatus. As these proteins move through the cisternae towards the maturing face, they undergo modification. Finally, the modified proteins are released from the concave trans (maturing) face of the Golgi apparatus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct logical sequence of events is: synthesis on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, fusion of ER vesicles with the cis face, modification within the Golgi cisternae, and release from the trans face, which corresponds to C, D, A, B.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q03 - Increasing order of cellular dimensions

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following cells in the correct increasing order of their typical size (from smallest to largest):

A. Human red blood cell
B. Typical eukaryotic cell
C. Mycoplasma
D. Typical bacterium

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four biological cell types are provided for size comparison: human red blood cell, typical eukaryotic cell, Mycoplasma, and typical bacterium.

Step 2: Quantitative Comparison of Cell Sizes
Mycoplasmas are the smallest cells, measuring only about \(0.3\;\mu\text{m}\) in length. Typical bacteria measure about \(1\text{--}2\;\mu\text{m}\) (or \(3\text{ to }5\;\mu\text{m}\)). Human red blood cells are about \(7.0\;\mu\text{m}\) in diameter. A typical eukaryotic cell measures about \(10\text{--}20\;\mu\text{m}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Ordering
Comparing the values in micrometres: \(0.3\;\mu\text{m} < 1\text{--}2\;\mu\text{m} < 7.0\;\mu\text{m} < 10\text{--}20\;\mu\text{m}\). Therefore, the size increases from Mycoplasma to a typical bacterium, then to a human red blood cell, and finally to a typical eukaryotic cell.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of size is C, D, A, B.
